title: When to Contact Your Care Team
learningGoals: Know that calling your care team is always okay, day or night
Recognize the labor pattern many care teams use as a signal to call
Know which symptoms mean call right away, without waiting for a pattern
Be ready with the information your care team will ask for
Save your own call card to your Birth Readiness Brief

review.notes: Reviewer: confirm the 5-1-1 framing matches the practices our learners use, and confirm each source page. Kick-count instructions are intentionally left out; the lesson teaches 'know your baby's normal and call if it changes' instead.

sources.title: How to Tell When Labor Begins (FAQ004)
Hear Her: Urgent Maternal Warning Signs

slides.heading: When to Contact Your Care Team
onScreen: Labor Basics · Lesson 2
About 10 minutes
slides.narration: Welcome back. In the last lesson, we talked about how labor begins. Now let's answer one of the most common questions in any childbirth class: when do I call? By the end of this lesson, you'll know the signals to watch for, the symptoms that mean call right away, and exactly what to say when you pick up the phone.

visual.description: Pregnant person on a couch at night, calmly holding a phone, support partner beside them with a notepad.

slides.heading: It's always okay to call
onScreen: Your care team expects these calls
Day or night, weekends included
Not sure? Call and ask
slides.narration: First, the most important message in this lesson: it is always okay to call. Many people wait until morning or try not to bother their doctor or midwife. But answering these calls is part of their job, at any hour. If you're not sure whether something is labor, or whether something is wrong, call. It's much better to get reassurance than to stay up worrying.

visual.description: Friendly nurse at a labor and delivery desk answering a phone at night, clock showing 3 AM.

slides.heading: Two kinds of calls
onScreen: Some calls can wait for a pattern. Some can't.
slides.narration: It helps to think about two kinds of calls. The first is a labor call. You make it when your contractions settle into the pattern your care team gave you. The second is a call right away. You make it for certain symptoms, like your water breaking, bleeding, or your baby moving less, no matter what your contractions are doing. Let's look at each one.
rows: You can't walk or talk through contractions
You've waited for the pattern to hold
Baby moving less, or not at all

visual.description: Two columns: left in calm teal labeled Labor call, right in alert red labeled Call right away.

slides.heading: The labor call: a common guideline
onScreen: Contractions 5 minutes apart or less
Each lasting about 1 minute
For at least 1 hour
Or: too strong to walk or talk through
slides.narration: Many midwives and doctors use a guideline called five, one, one. That means contractions coming five minutes apart or less, each lasting about one minute, for at least one hour. Another sign is when contractions get so strong that you can't walk or talk during them. But here's the key: your care team may give you a different rule. They might want a call sooner if this isn't your first baby, if past labors were fast, if you live far from your birth place, or because of your health history. Their instructions always come first.

visual.description: Large '5-1-1' graphic with three labeled parts: 5 minutes apart, 1 minute long, for 1 hour. Small note below: Your team's rule comes first.

question.prompt: Your contractions have been 5 minutes apart, each lasting about a minute, for the past hour. Your care team uses the 5-1-1 guideline. What should you do?
options: Wait another few hours to be sure
Only call if your water breaks
question.explanation: That's the 5-1-1 pattern, so it's time to call. Your care team will tell you whether to come in now or keep laboring at home a little longer.

slides.heading: Call right away: your water breaks
onScreen: Call even without contractions
Note the time
Note the color: clear, pink-tinged, green, or brown
Tell them if you tested positive for group B strep
slides.narration: If your water breaks, or you think it might have, call your care team, even if you aren't having any contractions. Note the time it happened and the color of the fluid. It's usually clear or slightly pink, but sometimes it's green or brown, and your team will want to know that. Also tell them if you tested positive for group B strep, a common bacteria checked near the end of pregnancy. If you did, you'll usually get antibiotics during labor to protect your baby.

visual.description: Four icons: phone, clock, color swatches (clear, pink, green, brown), and a small lab test tube labeled GBS.

slides.heading: Call right away: baby moving less
onScreen: Get to know your baby's normal pattern
If movement slows, changes, or stops, call
Babies should still move during labor
Don't wait to see if it improves
slides.narration: By the third trimester, you'll start to learn your baby's usual pattern of movement. Babies don't run out of room to move near the end of pregnancy, and they should keep moving even during labor. If your baby is moving less than usual, the pattern changes, or you can't feel movement, call your care team right away. Don't wait to see if it gets better, and don't try to reassure yourself at home first. Your team can check on your baby quickly.

visual.description: Pregnant person resting on their side with a hand on their belly, paying attention, calm expression.

slides.heading: Call right away: bleeding
onScreen: Pink or brownish mucus near term can be normal
Any other bleeding: call your care team
Heavy bleeding, like a period or more: call right away, or 911
slides.narration: In the last lesson, we talked about bloody show, the pink or brownish mucus that can come as your cervix starts to change. That can be normal. Any other bleeding, even spotting, is worth a call to your care team. And heavy bleeding, like a period or more, can be a sign of a serious problem. Call right away, and if it's heavy or you feel faint, call 911.

visual.description: Simple three-step scale from light to heavy: pink mucus (can be normal), spotting (call), heavy like a period (call now or 911). No graphic imagery.

slides.heading: Urgent warning signs: get help now
onScreen: Severe headache that won't go away, or vision changes
Trouble breathing, chest pain, or a racing heart
Severe belly pain that doesn't go away
Fever of 100.4°F or higher
Extreme swelling of hands or face
Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby
If it feels like an emergency, call 911
slides.narration: Some symptoms need help right away, whether or not you're in labor. These include a severe headache that won't go away or changes in your vision, trouble breathing, chest pain, or a racing heart, severe belly pain that doesn't go away, a fever of 100.4 degrees or higher, extreme swelling of your hands or face, and thoughts of harming yourself or your baby. If you have any of these, contact your care team immediately. If it feels like an emergency, call 911.

slides.heading: What to have ready when you call
onScreen: How many weeks pregnant you are
Your contraction times: how far apart, how long
If your water broke: when, and the color
Your group B strep result
Anything else you've noticed
slides.narration: When you call, the nurse or provider will ask a few questions. It helps to have the answers ready. They'll want to know how many weeks pregnant you are, how far apart your contractions are and how long they last, whether your water has broken and what it looked like, your group B strep result, and anything else you've noticed, like bleeding or changes in your baby's movement. This is a great job for a support person, so you can focus on breathing through contractions.

visual.description: Support partner on the phone reading from a notes app showing contraction times, pregnant person leaning on a counter nearby.

slides.heading: Hear a practice call
onScreen: Notice what the nurse asks, and how short the call can be
slides.narration: Let's listen in on a practice call so you know what to expect.

video.brief: Role-play: a support partner calls labor and delivery triage at night. The nurse asks weeks pregnant, contraction timing, water status and color, GBS result, baby's movement, and other symptoms. Nurse gives a calm decision (come in, or stay home and call back if X). Ends with the partner saying 'That was easier than I expected.' No specific clinical thresholds beyond what the lesson teaches.

slides.heading: Make your call card
onScreen: Daytime number for your care team
After-hours or labor and delivery number
Your group B strep result, once you know it
Who will call, and who will drive
slides.narration: Now let's make your call card. Write down your care team's daytime number, their after-hours or labor and delivery number, and your group B strep result once you have it. Decide who will make the call and who will drive. Save it here in your Birth Readiness Brief, and consider putting the numbers in both your phone and your support person's phone.
slides.prompt: Add your care team's daytime and after-hours numbers, your group B strep result, and who will call and drive.

slides.heading: Quick check-in
slides.narration: One more check-in before we wrap up.

question.prompt: At 39 weeks, your water breaks. You aren't having contractions, and the fluid looks greenish. What should you do?
options: Wait for contractions to start, then call
Call your care team now and tell them the fluid is greenish
Take a shower and rest first
question.explanation: Call now, even without contractions. Green or brown fluid is important for your care team to know, so be sure to mention the color and the time it happened.

slides.heading: What we covered
onScreen: It's always okay to call
Labor call: when contractions match your team's pattern
Call right away: water breaks, bleeding, baby moving less
Urgent warning signs: get help now, or call 911
Have your answers and your call card ready
slides.narration: Let's recap. It's always okay to call your care team. Make a labor call when your contractions match the pattern your team gave you. Call right away if your water breaks, if you have bleeding beyond light spotting, or if your baby is moving less. For urgent warning signs, get help immediately, or call 911. And have your call card ready before you need it. Next up, a few review questions.

reviewQuiz.prompt: Which of these is a reason to call your care team right away, without waiting for a contraction pattern?
options: Your baby is moving less than usual
You feel an occasional practice contraction
reviewQuiz.explanation: A change in your baby's movement is always worth an immediate call. Don't wait to see if it improves.

reviewQuiz.prompt: Your care team told you to call when contractions are 4 minutes apart, but a friend says 5-1-1 is the rule. Whose advice should you follow?
reviewQuiz.explanation: 5-1-1 is a common guideline, but your care team's instructions are based on your situation, so they always come first.

reviewQuiz.prompt: It's 2 AM and you're not sure if what you're feeling is labor. What's the best choice?
options: Call your care team's after-hours number
reviewQuiz.explanation: Care teams answer calls at all hours. If you're unsure, call. That's what they're there for.
